claims.text: Composition-dependent local lattice distortions govern intrinsic dislocation-glide resistance at low temperatures in equiatomic FCC concentrated alloys.
Mean-square atomic displacement (MSAD) sets the baseline critical resolved shear stress (CRSS).
At elevated temperatures, diffusible Mn- and Fe-rich solute atmospheres interact dynamically with dislocations through a Cottrell-type elastic attraction.
Dynamic interaction of Mn- and Fe-rich atmospheres with dislocations produces modest additional strengthening.
Dynamic solute pinning by Mn and Fe produces serrated flow associated with the Portevin–Le Chatelier effect.
Below room temperature, dislocation motion is controlled by thermally activated overcoming of solid-solution obstacles generated by lattice distortions.
Dislocation inertial effects moderate the rise in CRSS below approximately 60–77 K.
At high temperatures, diffusion of Mn and Fe forms atmospheres that transiently pin moving dislocations.
The proposed high-temperature solute-pinning mechanism occurs without significant changes in stacking-fault widths.
Cryogenic deformation will substantially increase CRSS relative to its room-temperature value.
The temperature dependence of the cryogenic CRSS increase will become less steep below approximately 77 K.
Between approximately 673 and 973 K, CRSS will exhibit a small but measurable increase relative to the intermediate-temperature baseline.
Deformation between approximately 673 and 973 K will exhibit serrated flow.
Alloys with higher MSAD will have higher extrapolated 0 K CRSS.
Cr-containing alloys have particularly high MSAD.
Alloys with greater Mn and Fe content will display a more pronounced Portevin–Le Chatelier effect.
CRSS is nearly temperature-independent in the intermediate-temperature regime before onset of the Portevin–Le Chatelier effect.
Diffusion-enabled Portevin–Le Chatelier behavior begins above approximately 673 K in the scoped alloy systems.
Magnetic transitions can affect MSAD measurements in alloys such as CrFeNi or FeCoNi.
Suzuki segregation may provide an alternative contribution to the proposed high-temperature behavior.
